title: Lottery Tax by State: What Winners Keep in 2026
description: Win a $200M Powerball jackpot? See exact take-home amounts after federal and state taxes in every state — real dollar figures, no vague estimates.
content:
Why Lottery Tax by State Determines Your Real Payout

If you won a $200 million Powerball jackpot tonight, here is exactly what you would take home in each state: anywhere from $50.4 million to $60.9 million as a lump sum after all taxes — a swing of more than $10 million depending entirely on where you live. That gap is not a rounding error. It is the direct result of lottery tax by state, and it is the single most important financial fact a winner needs to understand before they claim a single dollar.

This article uses a consistent $200 million Powerball jackpot as its base and walks through the complete federal and state tax math at every step. Every number here is a real dollar amount. Use our lottery tax calculator to run your own jackpot size and home state through the same math instantly.

How Federal Lottery Taxes Are Calculated — The Exact 37% Bite on a $200M Jackpot

Federal taxes hit every lottery winner the same way regardless of state. The IRS treats lottery winnings as ordinary income, which means a large jackpot pushes the winner into the top federal bracket immediately. Here is how the numbers work on a $200 million advertised jackpot.

Step 1: The Lump Sum Cash Value

Powerball's lump sum cash option is approximately 60% of the advertised jackpot. On a $200 million prize, that means the before-tax cash value is $96.6 million. This is the number all subsequent tax calculations are based on.

Step 2: Immediate Federal Withholding at 24%

The IRS requires lottery operators to withhold 24% of prizes over $5,000 at the time of payment. On $96.6 million, that withholding is $23.2 million, leaving the winner with $73.4 million in hand before filing their tax return.

Step 3: The True Federal Rate at Filing — 37%

Withholding is not the final federal bill. When the winner files their tax return, the full $96.6 million is taxed as ordinary income. The top federal marginal rate of 37% applies to income above $626,350 for single filers — and virtually the entire jackpot lump sum clears that threshold. The total federal tax owed is $35.7 million. After crediting the $23.2 million already withheld, the winner owes an additional $12.5 million at filing. Net federal take-home after all federal taxes: $60.9 million.

This assumes a single filer with no other significant income offsets, deductions, or credits. Individual circumstances vary.

Lump Sum vs. Annuity — Real Dollar Difference After Taxes on a $200M Powerball Win

Powerball offers winners a choice: take the lump sum now or receive the full $200 million paid out as 30 annual payments over 29 years, with each payment increasing by 5% per year.

Lump Sum After All Taxes (No State Tax State)

As calculated above, the federal-only take-home on the lump sum is $60.9 million. In a no-state-tax state like Florida or Texas, that is your final number: $60.9 million in a single payment.

Annuity After All Taxes (No State Tax State)

With the annuity, the full $200 million is paid out, but each annual check is also taxed as ordinary income at the 37% federal rate (once total income clears the top bracket threshold, which it will on every payment). The first-year payment on a $200 million Powerball annuity is approximately $3.0 million before taxes, rising to roughly $10.4 million by year 30. After federal taxes at 37%, the total net annuity payout over 29 years in a no-tax state is approximately $126 million — more than double the lump sum take-home in raw dollar terms.

The trade-off is time and certainty. The lump sum delivers $60.9 million today. The annuity delivers $126 million spread over three decades, with no guarantee of future tax rates. Most financial advisors note that the lump sum's investment potential can close much of that gap — but that calculation depends heavily on individual investment returns. Consult a financial advisor before making this decision.

The difference between winning in New York vs. Florida on a $200M Powerball jackpot lump sum is more than $10.5 million — just from state taxes alone.

The 9 States With No State Lottery Tax — How Much More Winners Keep

Nine states impose zero state income tax on lottery winnings. In all nine, the federal-only take-home of $60.9 million on a $200 million lump sum is the final number. These states are:

  • California — no state tax on lottery winnings (California lottery taxes)
  • Florida — no state income tax
  • New Hampshire — no state income tax on wages or lottery winnings
  • Pennsylvania — lottery winnings specifically exempt from state income tax
  • South Dakota — no state income tax
  • Tennessee — no state income tax
  • Texas — no state income tax
  • Washington — no state income tax
  • Wyoming — no state income tax

Compared to a winner in New York, a winner in any of these nine states keeps an additional $10.5 million on the same $200 million jackpot. That is not a tax planning trick — it is simply the state where the winning ticket was purchased and where the winner is a legal resident at the time of the claim.

The 5 Worst States for Lottery Taxes — Dollar-by-Dollar Breakdown

These five states extract the most from a lottery winner. All figures use the $96.6 million lump sum before state taxes, after federal taxes of $35.7 million have been applied.

1. New York — 10.9% State Tax

State tax: $10,529,400. Final take-home: $50,370,600. New York City residents face an additional city tax of up to 3.876%, which could reduce take-home by another $3.7 million. See New York lottery taxes for the full city-level breakdown.

2. New Jersey — 10.75% State Tax

State tax: $10,384,500. Final take-home: $50,515,500. New Jersey's rate is a flat 10.75% on lottery winnings over $10,000, making it the second most expensive state for large jackpot winners.

3. Oregon — 9.9% State Tax

State tax: $9,563,400. Final take-home: $51,336,600. Oregon's top income tax rate of 9.9% applies to lottery winnings, putting it in the top three most expensive states for winners.

4. Minnesota — 9.85% State Tax

State tax: $9,515,100. Final take-home: $51,384,900. Minnesota's rate is just a fraction behind Oregon's, but on a $96.6 million lump sum, that fraction still represents nearly $9.5 million going to the state.

5. Maryland — 8.75% State Tax

State tax: $8,452,500. Final take-home: $52,447,500. Maryland's 8.75% rate rounds out the five worst states, costing winners over $8.4 million more than a winner in a no-tax state keeps.
